title: The Argument from Undesigned Coincidences

keyTerms.d: A particular shape of fit between two texts. One account mentions a detail that, on its own, is puzzling or incomplete; a second account, written for unrelated purposes and showing no awareness of the first’s difficulty, contains an offhand detail that resolves it. The fit is too specific to be likely chance, yet too casual and unflagged to look planted.

The argument is an inference to the best explanation, not a deductive proof. No premise guarantees its conclusion; the cases raise the probability of reliability, they do not establish it with certainty.

No single coincidence is meant to carry weight; any one of them might be chance or might have a mundane literary explanation. The argument lives or dies on the pattern — many cases, of the right shape, pointing the same direction.

The probability of the interlocking pattern is high if the reports are well-informed and substantially independent, and low if they are invented or derived from a single tidy source. That likelihood gap is the whole engine of the argument, and Lydia McGrew frames it explicitly in the language of probability.

The genuine cases are not mere “fits”: one text raises a specific oddity (why Philip?) that it never resolves, and another casually resolves it. That asymmetric structure is considerably rarer than a loose thematic resemblance, and harder to generate by chance trawling.

On the standard two-source hypothesis, Mark was written first and Matthew and Luke both used Mark. If a coincidence holds only between texts in a known dependence relation — especially Mark and a Gospel that used Mark — redaction is a live alternative explanation, and such cases carry less weight.

Paley’s original domain, which many defenders regard as the strongest of all: small, oblique agreements between Paul’s letters and Acts. But the premise that Acts is independent of the letters can no longer be presented as settled — Richard Pervo, Joseph Tyson and the Acts Seminar argue that its author knew and mined the letters.

The quality of reading like truthful report from the inside. Undesigned coincidences are best understood as a contributor to it — corroboration, not proof: they build credibility for well-informed testimony, but do not by themselves establish that what it reports is true.

derive.q: Two witnesses to a car accident each mention, unprompted and for unrelated reasons, that the streetlight was out — their convergence is striking because…?
derive.ans: neither was trying to corroborate the other
derive.why: Detectives, historians, and courts routinely treat accounts that agree at incidental, uncoordinated points as more credible than accounts that agree only on the headline. Coordinated liars produce agreement on the main story; what they rarely produce is a web of small, mutually explanatory details that none of them flagged.

derive.q: A later author copying a source notices a connection in it — the natural editorial move is to…?
derive.ans: state it — make the link explicit for the reader
derive.why: That is what tidying looks like: to clarify, to smooth, to make the link explicit. The strong undesigned coincidences do the opposite — the explaining detail sits in a different document, dropped for an unrelated reason, with neither writer flagging the link. That the reader has to assemble it is precisely what redaction does not predict.

derive.q: If John knew Mark, the “green grass”/Passover fit could be…?
derive.ans: a designed inference, not an undesigned coincidence
derive.why: John could simply have read Mark’s “green grass,” inferred the rainy spring season, and added his own note that Passover was near. If John knew Mark, the case should be dropped from the load-bearing cases. But that move has no purchase on cases where the explanatory detail is buried in an unrelated context for an unrelated reason.

derive.q: The company travelling with Paul (Acts 20:4) adds two men from Asia and no one from Achaia — does that imperfect fit with the letters count against the case…?
derive.ans: no — it reads like a separate record of the same enterprise
derive.why: The letters never enroll Asia in the collection, and they press Achaia’s gift hardest. A harmoniser stitching Acts to the letters would have matched the provinces cleanly and supplied the missing Corinthian; the actual list, loose in both directions, reads like a separate record. Acts gives the roster; the letters give the reason; neither points to the other.

derive.q: Defenders have not counted the misses — so are the interlocks just chance fits…?
derive.ans: no — a gap in bookkeeping, not a defeater
derive.why: The concession is real: defenders have not, on the whole, done the rigorous work of counting misses, and quantifying the pattern remains the argument’s least developed flank. But the genuine cases are question-and-answer shaped, which is considerably rarer than a loose thematic resemblance; a missing count does not turn question-and-answer interlocks into chance fits.

derive.q: Granting every strong case, does the argument show the miracles happened…?
derive.ans: no — corroboration of the testimony, not proof of miracles
derive.why: The coincidences mostly touch the mundane scaffolding of the narratives — geography, names, seasons, court gossip — and the credibility they build must be carried over to the extraordinary claims by separate argument. Whether what that testimony reports is true, up to and including Easter morning, is made on its own ground, in the historical case for the resurrection.

honestState.p1: This is not, at present, a front-line debate in academic New Testament studies. The argument has enthusiastic defenders — Lydia McGrew foremost, with endorsements from scholars such as Craig Keener and the apologist J. Warner Wallace — and energetic popular critics, of whom Richard Carrier is the most prominent; but it has not generated a large peer-reviewed literature pro or con. McGrew’s most rigorous statement is an article in the philosophy journal Erkenntnis on the formal logic of varied, dovetailing evidence — a treatment of the formal logic rather than a verse-by-verse defense. The mainstream guild has largely not engaged the revived argument, and a fair observer should treat that silence as neither endorsement nor refutation. The live, unsettled questions are how much the consensus of literary dependence erodes the cross-Gospel cases, whether the pattern survives a properly disciplined accounting of hits and misses, and — since Pervo, Tyson and the Acts Seminar argue that Acts mined Paul’s letters — whether the Acts–Epistles tier is as independent as the traditional reasoning held.
honestState.fairness: Honest defenders must concede that where a coincidence holds only between texts in a known dependence relation — especially Mark and a Gospel that used Mark — redaction is a live alternative and such cases carry less weight; that the green-grass case should be dropped from the load-bearing cases if John used Mark; that defenders have not, on the whole, done the rigorous work of counting misses; and that the independence of Acts from the letters can no longer be presented as settled. McGrew herself accepts this discipline, treating different cases as having different strengths. But the dependence move does not reach the strongest cases: a copyist who spots a link states it, while the strong cases bury the explaining detail in a different document for an unrelated reason — and on the Acts–Epistles material, the shape of the agreements is not what literary borrowing predicts. A missing count of misses is a gap in the defense’s bookkeeping, not a defeater.
honestState.verdict: Undesigned coincidences are best understood as a contributor to verisimilitude and, where the strongest cases hold, as positive evidence that the Gospels and Acts rest on well-informed, substantially independent sources rather than on late legend or a single coordinated fabrication. After the appropriate concessions, the case rests most securely on the Acts–Epistles material and the best-shaped cross-Gospel cases, not on every example ever paraded — so the claim in Carrier’s title does not hold: the dependence move deflates the weaker cases, but the best-shaped ones survive it. It is real but contested evidence, and it is bounded: it does not prove the Gospels inerrant, and it does not by itself establish that any miracle occurred. That is corroboration, not proof. Whether what that testimony reports is true — up to and including Easter morning — is argued on its own ground, in the historical case for the resurrection.

order: When two accounts interlock — one casually answering a question the other leaves open, with no sign of contrivance — the best explanation is that both report real events that the writers actually knew.
The Gospels and Acts contain many such undesigned coincidences: offhand details in one account that unintentionally explain puzzles in another.
Therefore, these documents are best explained as well-informed, substantially independent testimony to real events, not as late legend or coordinated invention.

cards.a: A detail in one account that, on its own, is puzzling or incomplete, resolved by an offhand detail in a second account written for unrelated purposes and showing no awareness of the first’s difficulty. The fit is too specific to be likely chance, yet too casual and unflagged to look planted.

cards.q: What kind of argument is this — and where does its force lie?
cards.a: An inference to the best explanation, not a deductive proof: the cases raise the probability of reliability, they do not establish it with certainty. And the force is cumulative — no single coincidence carries weight; the argument lives or dies on the pattern.

cards.q: Why is the Philip-and-Bethsaida case among the cleanest?
cards.a: John alone has Jesus ask Philip where to buy bread; Luke places the feeding near Bethsaida; and John, chapters earlier and for an unrelated reason, notes Philip was from Bethsaida. The explaining detail sits in a different part of John, the geographical anchor comes from a different Gospel altogether — and no Gospel draws the link.

cards.q: Why should the “green grass” case be held loosely?
cards.a: Mark’s green grass and John’s nearby Passover cohere, since the grass is green only briefly in spring. But this is where the literary-dependence objection bites hardest: if John knew Mark, he could have inferred the season from Mark, so the case should be conceded as weak if John used Mark and dropped from the load-bearing cases.

cards.q: What does the Herod’s-court cluster show?
cards.a: Matthew alone has Herod speak about Jesus “to his servants” (14:2); Luke, incidentally, names among Jesus’ supporters Joanna, wife of Herod’s household manager, and Acts adds Manaen, brought up with Herod. The movement had inside connections to Herod’s household, which would explain how it could report what went on there; none of the texts points out the link.

cards.q: How do Paul’s letters and Acts 20:4 interlock over the collection for Jerusalem?
cards.a: The letters are preoccupied with a relief fund to be carried by accredited delegates; Acts barely mentions it, yet names, without explaining why, a company travelling with Paul. Acts gives the roster; the letters give the reason; neither points to the other. And the fit is loose in both directions — two Asians added, no one from Achaia — where a harmoniser would have matched the provinces cleanly.

cards.q: What does the literary-dependence objection rightly force a defender to concede?
cards.a: That where a coincidence holds only between texts in a known dependence relation — especially Mark and a Gospel that used Mark — redaction is a live alternative and such cases carry less weight. A defender cannot simply wave away Markan priority, the majority view; McGrew herself treats cases as having different strengths and sets aside ones too weak to lean on.

cards.q: Why doesn’t redaction explain the strongest cases?
cards.a: When a later author notices a connection in his source, the natural editorial move is to state it. The strong cases do the opposite: the explaining detail sits in a different document, dropped for an unrelated reason, with neither writer flagging the link. And the strongest cross-Gospel cases draw the explaining detail from a Gospel not in the relevant source relation.

cards.q: A critic says the author of Acts simply mined Paul’s letters. Your reply?
cards.a: Dependence has not been ruled out, but Acts does not behave like a document built out of the letters: it never verbatim-quotes them and diverges where a borrower would lean on his source — suggestive rather than decisive. The real weight falls on the shape of the agreements: harmonizers connect the dots; these texts leave them unconnected.

cards.q: A critic says John invented Philip’s hometown to fit the feeding’s location. Your reply?
cards.a: John’s own feeding scene never names Bethsaida, and Philip’s hometown sits five chapters earlier in a disciple-list, with no signal pointing forward. An inventor cashes in his invention; he does not bury the one detail that makes it pay. The alternative is available in principle but far less economical than that John simply knew it.

cards.q: What must be conceded on selection bias — and what still stands?
cards.a: Defenders have not, on the whole, done the rigorous work of counting misses; quantifying the pattern remains the argument’s least developed flank. But the genuine cases are question-and-answer shaped, which is rarer and harder to generate by chance trawling — so a missing count is a gap in the bookkeeping, not a defeater.

cards.q: What does the argument establish — and what does it NOT?
cards.a: Where the strongest cases hold, positive evidence that the Gospels and Acts rest on well-informed, substantially independent sources rather than late legend — corroboration, not proof. It does not prove inerrancy, which no historical argument can settle either way, and does not by itself establish any miracle; surface tensions are themselves evidence the writers were not colluding. Whether the testimony is true is argued on its own ground, in the historical case for the resurrection.

obj.q: Richard Carrier says there are no undesigned coincidences, and that your “safest” tier is the first to fall: “Obviously the author of Acts used those Epistles as a source text.” Pervo and the Acts Seminar date Acts to the early second century and argue its author mined Paul’s letters. Then every Acts–Epistles interlock is deliberate borrowing dressed up as independent memory.
obj.model: That has to be met on the merits, not by waving the dependence question away — and it is true that the independence of Acts from the letters can no longer be presented as settled. So grant the premise for the sake of argument: suppose the author of Acts had read Paul’s letters. The trouble is that Acts does not behave like a document built out of them. It never verbatim-quotes the letters — not once — and at the points where a borrower would most want to lean on his source, Acts diverges from it: Galatians has Paul go away into Arabia rather than up to Jerusalem (Gal 1:17), while Acts narrates a prompt visit to Jerusalem and a different sequence of trips. That should not be overstated — a redactor with a theological agenda can diverge deliberately, so the divergences are suggestive rather than decisive. The real weight falls on the shape of the agreements. Over the collection for Jerusalem, Acts gives the roster (Acts 20:4) and the letters give the reason, neither pointing to the other, and the fit is loose in both directions where a harmoniser would have matched the provinces cleanly. Harmonizers connect the dots; these texts leave them unconnected. So the Acts–Epistles material survives the objection — not because dependence has been ruled out a priori, but because the pattern fits independent knowledge better than it fits a redactor reworking the letters.

obj.q: Carrier names your flagship case. Philip and Bethsaida are not two independent witnesses: John found the feeding placed near Bethsaida in Mark and Luke, made Philip a native of the town, and wrote Jesus’ question to Philip on the strength of it. That is invention fitted to a source, not an undesigned coincidence.
obj.model: An invented detail does its work only if the reader can see what it is for, and John never lets the reader see it. His own feeding scene never names Bethsaida at all — John 6:1 places it only on “the other side of the Sea of Galilee” — so the location Carrier says John was fitting appears nowhere in John’s account. The load-bearing detail, that Philip was “from Bethsaida,” sits in John 1, five chapters earlier, inside a disciple-list, planted for the unrelated purpose of introducing Andrew and Peter, with no narrative signal pointing forward to the feeding; and when John mentions Philip’s hometown again (John 12:21) he still draws no connection. On Carrier’s telling, John manufactured both the hometown and the question and hid the join, so that it pays off only for a reader who lays Luke 9:10 beside John 1:44. That is the opposite of how invention for effect works: an inventor cashes in his invention; he does not bury the one detail that makes it pay. Carrier’s alternative is available in principle, but it is a far less economical hypothesis than that John simply knew Philip was from Bethsaida. On this case, Carrier’s reading does not hold.

obj.q: On the standard two-source hypothesis Matthew and Luke used Mark, and a growing number of scholars think John knew Mark too. Then John could have read Mark’s “green grass,” inferred spring, and added that Passover was near. Your coincidences are redaction — a later author working from an earlier text — and the whole method is an anachronism from before source criticism.
obj.model: The honest concession is large. If a coincidence holds only between texts in a known dependence relation — especially Mark and a Gospel that used Mark — redaction is a live alternative, and such cases carry less weight; a defender cannot simply wave away Markan priority, the majority view. On the green grass, the reply is mostly to retreat: if John knew Mark, that link may indeed be a designed inference rather than an undesigned coincidence, and it should be dropped from the load-bearing cases. McGrew herself accepts this discipline, treating cases as having different strengths. But notice what the move does not reach. It turns on a writer drawing an easy inference from a detail his source highlights; it has no purchase on cases where the explanatory detail is buried in an unrelated context for an unrelated reason. A copyist who spotted the link would state it; the strong cases leave the reader to assemble it, which is precisely what redaction does not predict — and the strongest cross-Gospel cases, like Philip and Bethsaida, draw the explaining detail from a Gospel not in the relevant source relation. So the objection deflates the weaker cases, and the argument rests on the strong ones — on which the dependence move, even when granted its premises, predicts the wrong shape.

obj.q: Search any two long, overlapping texts and you will find details in one that seem to “explain” the other by sheer chance. Defenders parade the hits and never count the misses — how many puzzles in one Gospel find no answer in another, how often the accounts flatly conflict. Without a denominator, a pile of impressive-looking fits tells us nothing.
obj.model: This is a genuine methodological worry, and it calls for a real concession: defenders have not, on the whole, done the rigorous work of counting misses, and the argument would be stronger if they had. The probabilistic framing helps but does not fully answer it. What can be said is twofold. First, the genuine cases are not mere “fits” but question-and-answer shaped — one text raises a specific oddity (why Philip?) that it never resolves, and another casually resolves it. That asymmetric structure is considerably rarer than a loose thematic resemblance, and harder to generate by chance trawling. Second, the claim is not that one fit is decisive but that the number and specificity of well-shaped cases, concentrated in documents purporting to report the same events, is what an honest-and-informed hypothesis predicts and a fabrication hypothesis does not. As for apparent conflicts, they belong to the count the defence has not yet done; the narrower point the essay makes is that surface tensions are themselves evidence the writers were not colluding — a point about independence, not a claim that every conflict dissolves. Quantifying the pattern remains the argument’s least developed flank — but that is a gap in the defense’s bookkeeping, not a defeater: a missing count does not turn question-and-answer interlocks into chance fits. So the objection does not sink the argument.

unseen.q: If undesigned coincidences were real evidence, New Testament scholars would be using them. The method went out with Paley and Blunt, and the guild has ignored its revival — there is no large peer-reviewed literature on it. That silence is the verdict.
unseen.model: It must be said plainly that this is not, at present, a front-line debate in academic New Testament studies, and that fact cuts in more than one direction. The argument went quiet for over a century, neglected as biblical scholarship turned to source and form criticism. Its modern revival, above all Lydia McGrew’s, restated the case with explicit probabilistic reasoning and direct engagement with the objection from literary dependence, and her most rigorous statement is a peer-reviewed article in the philosophy journal Erkenntnis on the formal logic of varied, dovetailing evidence — a treatment of the formal logic rather than a verse-by-verse defense. It has endorsements from scholars such as Craig Keener, and energetic popular critics, of whom Richard Carrier is the most prominent — but it has not generated a large peer-reviewed literature pro or con. The mainstream guild has largely not engaged the revived argument, and a fair observer should treat that silence as neither endorsement nor refutation. So the silence settles nothing either way: the cases must be weighed on their merits, as real but contested evidence, not as a settled result.
